theme: Job’s response; restoration, the answer is a person
readingInstruction: Read Job 40:1-42:17. This is the end of the book. Job answers God, God speaks again, and then there is an epilogue in prose. Pay special attention to Job’s confession in 42:1-6, and to what God says about Job and his friends in 42:7-9.
settingTheScene: Yesterday God began to speak. Today he finishes. Job has been silent through the first round of questions, and now God presses him again. He describes two great creatures, Behemoth and Leviathan, which are beyond Job’s power to control. Then Job speaks for the last time, and the book moves into its quiet ending. In the prologue you were allowed to see what Job could not. In the epilogue Job sees something that you cannot see unless you have been through what he has: God himself.
observation: God asks, “Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty?” (40:2). Job answers, “Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth” (40:4).
God speaks again and asks, “Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?” (40:8).
Behemoth is described as “the first of the works of God” (40:19), strong enough to be calm when the river rages.
Leviathan is a creature no one can capture or tame. God says, “Who then is he who can stand before me?” (41:10) and calls him “king over all the sons of pride” (41:34).
Job answers, “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted” (42:2).
He admits that he spoke of things beyond him: “Things too wonderful for me, which I did not know” (42:3).
“I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (42:5-6).
God tells Eliphaz, “My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (42:7).
Job prays for his friends, and the LORD restores his fortunes and gives him twice as much as he had before (42:8-10).
Job has seven sons and three daughters again, and he lives 140 years, “old and full of days” (42:13-17).
interpretation:
The final answer of the book is not an argument. It is an encounter. Job says it directly: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” Before, Job had a faith made of reports and reasoning. He knew the right things about God. Now he has seen him. The suffering did not give Job a reason. It gave him God. That is not a consolation prize. It is the greatest thing that a person can receive.

His repentance needs careful reading. He does not repent of the sins his friends accused him of, because those were false. He repents of speaking about things he did not understand, of treating God as a defendant in his case. “I despise myself” might also be translated “I retract” or “I submit.” He sees how small he is, and how much he had assumed. This is not groveling. It is the right posture of a creature who has seen the Creator.

The surprise in 42:7 is that God vindicates Job over his friends. “You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.” How could this be, when Job said such bold and bitter things? The answer seems to be that Job spoke to God, honestly, while the friends spoke about God, dishonestly. They defended him with false claims. Job wrestled with him with true ones. God prefers honest wrestling to false piety.

Notice the next detail. Job prays for the friends who hurt him. The restoration comes after that prayer. The man who longed for a mediator now becomes one. It is a small picture of what Christ will do on a larger scale.

The restoration is real, but it is not the point. The children who died are not replaced, and the new ones are not substitutes for the old. The book does not say that suffering always ends in earthly blessing. But it does say that God is faithful, and that his last word is never the grave.
connection: James 5:11 says, “You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.” Isaiah 6:5 records a similar response from Isaiah, who sees the Lord and says, “Woe is me!” Paul prays that we might know Christ and the power of his resurrection (Philippians 3:10). Jesus prays for those who persecute him (Luke 23:34).
application:
Think about the difference between knowing about God and knowing him. Which describes you more? Ask God to give you the second.

If someone has wronged you, pray for them this week by name. It may be hard. Do it anyway.

Also, remember that God prefers honest prayer to polite prayer. If you have been holding back what you actually think, tell him.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to see him and not only hear of him.
Confess any place where you have spoken of what you do not understand.
Ask him to teach you to pray for those who have hurt you.
